title: Well-Child Care: Growth, Development, Prevention, and Family Priorities
bottomLine: Well-child care is longitudinal surveillance, not a checklist of normal findings. Track growth and development over time, update immunization and screening, identify family/social risks, provide age-specific anticipatory guidance and act early when a trajectory or caregiver concern is abnormal.
recognize: Growth velocity, developmental progression, school/function, sleep, nutrition, oral health, safety and family context matter more than one isolated percentile or milestone.
Caregiver concern can be an important developmental signal even when a brief office interaction appears reassuring.
differentiate: Screening/surveillance identifies risk; a positive screen requires diagnostic evaluation and referral rather than simply repeating reassurance.
Normal developmental variation differs from loss of previously acquired skills, which is a red flag.
assessment: Review growth curves, development, hearing/vision, nutrition, sleep, elimination, school/behaviour, mental health, family/social determinants, injury prevention and immunization status.
workup: Use age- and risk-appropriate screening tools/tests rather than a universal laboratory panel.
Investigate faltering growth, developmental delay or abnormal examination according to the pattern and trajectory.
management: Provide anticipatory guidance matched to age and family priorities, update prevention and make referrals early when developmental, social or medical risk is identified.
medicationSafety: Confirm weight-based dosing and avoid unnecessary OTC cough/cold or sedating products in young children.
redFlags: Severe caregiver mental-health or access crisis affecting child safety
counselling: Use strengths-based, culturally safe guidance and prioritize a few actionable topics rather than overwhelming families.
followUp: Track unresolved screening/referral issues to closure and compare growth/development longitudinally.
examTrap: Calling a single normal exam sufficient despite developmental regression or a clear caregiver concern.
oneLinePearl: Well-child care is about trajectories and prevention, not one normal visit.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society preventive-care and child-development resources
Rourke Baby Record Canadian preventive-care framework

title: Pediatric Immunization and Catch-Up: Use Current NACI Guidance, Do Not Restart Delayed Series
bottomLine: Pediatric immunization is governed by current NACI/Canadian Immunization Guide recommendations plus provincial or territorial delivery programs. Delayed series are generally continued rather than restarted; age, risk, prior valid doses, pregnancy and immune status determine the catch-up plan.
recognize: National recommendations and publicly funded provincial schedules are related but not identical.
Immunocompromise, asplenia, travel and outbreak exposure can create additional vaccine needs.
differentiate: Expected local/systemic vaccine reactions are not vaccine allergy.
Minor illness is usually not a reason to defer routine immunization, while selected live vaccines are contraindicated in significant immunosuppression or pregnancy.
assessment: Review reliable records, age, prior doses/intervals, medical risks, pregnancy, immune status, travel, adverse reactions and access barriers.
workup: Serology is used only for selected indications; do not order broad immunity panels when catch-up vaccination is the appropriate route.
management: Use current CIG/NACI minimum intervals and vaccine-specific guidance and coordinate with the local funded schedule.
Do not restart a valid interrupted series solely because time has elapsed.
medicationSafety: Timing with immunoglobulin/blood products and immunosuppressive therapies can affect live-vaccine safety/effectiveness.
Check the current 2026 guidance where product recommendations changed, including RSV and meningococcal prevention.
counselling: Give a clear recommendation, address specific concerns, explain national versus local-program differences and avoid shame about delayed vaccines.
followUp: Document doses and schedule remaining catch-up doses using the jurisdictional registry when available.
examTrap: Restarting an entire vaccine series because the child is years late—or using a memorized schedule despite a 2026 NACI update.
oneLinePearl: Delayed vaccine series continue; current NACI guidance beats memory.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada Canadian Immunization Guide
National Advisory Committee on Immunization 2026 statements

title: Newborn Care and Screening: Transition, Feeding, Jaundice, Safety, and Follow-Up
bottomLine: Early newborn care is a transition assessment: feeding, weight, hydration, jaundice, cardiorespiratory adaptation, temperature, infection risk and completion of provincial newborn screening. Age in hours, gestational age and trajectory determine urgency; a well appearance does not erase neonatal risk.
recognize: Feeding difficulty, excessive weight loss, reduced urine/stool, worsening jaundice or temperature instability can be early disease clues.
Newborn screening programs vary by province/territory and require closed-loop result follow-up.
differentiate: Physiologic transition differs from respiratory distress, sepsis, critical congenital heart disease or pathologic jaundice.
Bilirubin and glucose thresholds in newborns are age/gestation/risk dependent and should not use adult values.
assessment: Review gestational/birth history, maternal infections/medications, feeding, weight change, urine/stool, jaundice, temperature, tone, breathing, heart/pulses and family supports.
workup: Use bilirubin, glucose, pulse-ox/other newborn screening and infection evaluation according to age, risk and local program.
Confirm metabolic/hearing/other provincial screening is completed and results are traceable.
management: Support feeding and thermal care, address jaundice/glucose issues using age-specific pathways and escalate respiratory, infectious, cardiac or neurologic abnormalities promptly.
medicationSafety: Avoid casual medication exposure in newborns; dosing and contraindications are age-specific and breastfeeding exposures require context.
counselling: Teach feeding/diaper expectations, safe sleep, jaundice/illness warning signs and how/when screening results will be communicated.
followUp: Arrange early newborn follow-up based on discharge timing, feeding/weight, jaundice and social risk; own pending screening results.
examTrap: Reassuring a poorly feeding newborn because the temperature is normal or because the baby looked well at discharge.
oneLinePearl: Newborn risk is age-in-hours plus trajectory plus physiology—not appearance alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society newborn-care guidance
Provincial/territorial newborn screening programs

title: Infant Feeding and Nutrition: Growth, Intake, Development, and Family Choice
bottomLine: Infant feeding assessment combines growth trajectory, hydration, feeding mechanics, developmental readiness and family goals. Support breastfeeding/chestfeeding, formula or mixed feeding safely without moralizing; identify poor transfer, micronutrient risk or unsafe preparation early.
recognize: Adequate intake is reflected by hydration, diaper pattern, satiety and appropriate growth trajectory rather than feed duration alone.
Complementary foods are introduced based on developmental readiness and nutrition needs, with iron-rich foods important in infancy.
differentiate: Normal cluster feeding differs from poor milk transfer with dehydration/weight loss.
Reflux/spit-up differs from bilious vomiting, forceful progressive emesis, blood or faltering growth.
assessment: Review birth history, feeding method/frequency, latch/transfer or bottle technique, formula preparation, vitamin supplementation, urine/stool, vomiting, allergy symptoms and growth.
workup: No routine labs are required for a thriving infant; investigate faltering growth, anemia risk, dehydration or suspected disease according to phenotype.
management: Provide skilled lactation/feeding support when desired, ensure safe formula preparation and age-appropriate complementary feeding, and correct specific nutrient risks.
medicationSafety: Avoid honey before 12 months and unsafe homemade formula dilution/concentration; review medication/herbal products used to alter milk supply for evidence and safety.
redFlags: Blood in stool with systemic illness
counselling: Use nonjudgmental feeding counselling and account for food insecurity, culture and caregiver capacity.
followUp: Recheck weight/feeding after significant intervention and close referrals for swallowing/feeding or medical causes.
examTrap: Assuming frequent breastfeeding means inadequate supply without assessing transfer, diapers and growth—or dismissing faltering growth as a feeding preference issue.
oneLinePearl: Infant feeding success is safe intake plus growth and family sustainability.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society infant nutrition resources
Health Canada infant feeding guidance

title: Childhood Growth and Development: Follow the Trajectory, Not One Percentile
bottomLine: Growth and development are longitudinal processes. Interpret height, weight/BMI/head circumference where age-appropriate and milestones against prior trajectory, genetic context, puberty and function; crossing trajectories, developmental regression or disproportion warrants explanation.
recognize: A child can be healthy at a low or high percentile when growth velocity and context are appropriate.
Pubertal timing alters growth velocity and body composition.
differentiate: Constitutional delay/familial stature differs from endocrine, GI, renal, inflammatory, nutritional or psychosocial growth failure.
Developmental delay is not diagnosed from one missed milestone without considering the broader domain pattern, but regression is always concerning.
assessment: Plot serial growth accurately and assess nutrition, chronic symptoms, bowel pattern, sleep, medications, family heights/puberty, psychosocial stress and developmental domains.
workup: Target testing to the growth pattern—e.g., disproportion, weight-first or height-first change, systemic symptoms or pubertal abnormalities—rather than ordering a universal short-stature panel.
management: Address nutritional/social causes, treat chronic disease and refer endocrinology/genetics/developmental services when pattern or severity warrants.
medicationSafety: Chronic corticosteroids/stimulants and other therapies can affect growth; review benefit, dose and monitoring without stopping needed treatment abruptly.
counselling: Discuss trajectory and function rather than labelling body size as failure or success.
followUp: Repeat standardized measurements at an interval suited to the suspected problem and ensure referrals are completed.
examTrap: Ordering growth-hormone testing from one short height measurement without reviewing growth velocity, parental height and puberty.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric growth is a curve, not a dot.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society growth and development resources
WHO/Canadian growth-chart practice

title: Developmental Surveillance and Screening: Concern Is a Reason to Act
bottomLine: Developmental surveillance occurs at every child encounter; validated screening is added at recommended ages or when concern arises. A positive screen or credible caregiver concern should trigger evaluation/referral and hearing/vision/medical review rather than repeated watchful waiting when delay could cost early intervention time.
recognize: Language, social, motor, cognitive/adaptive and emotional domains can be affected independently or together.
Regression or loss of skills is distinct from slow acquisition and raises neurologic/metabolic concern.
differentiate: Screening identifies risk and is not a definitive diagnosis.
Language delay can reflect hearing loss, autism, developmental language disorder, global delay or environmental factors and deserves differentiation.
assessment: Elicit caregiver concerns, observe interaction/play/motor skills and review milestones, hearing/vision, sleep, nutrition, family/developmental history and psychosocial context.
workup: Use validated tools and targeted hearing/vision/medical/genetic testing when indicated by the pattern.
Do not delay referral for early intervention while waiting for every diagnostic label.
management: Refer developmental/therapy services promptly for significant concern and coordinate school/community supports.
Escalate regression, seizures or abnormal neurologic findings to specialist assessment.
medicationSafety: Avoid using medication to manage nonspecific behaviour before defining developmental, sleep, communication and environmental contributors.
counselling: Explain that referral does not equal a diagnosis and early supports are beneficial while assessment proceeds.
followUp: Track referral completion and developmental progress rather than documenting 'monitor' indefinitely.
examTrap: Repeating reassurance after a positive developmental screen because the child made eye contact briefly during the visit.
oneLinePearl: Developmental concern is an action signal, not a reason to wait for certainty.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society developmental surveillance resources

title: Autism Screening: Social-Communication Pattern, Repetitive Behaviour, and Early Referral
bottomLine: Autism screening identifies children who need diagnostic assessment; it does not diagnose autism by questionnaire alone. Persistent social-communication differences, restricted/repetitive behaviour, sensory differences or regression should trigger developmental referral and hearing/medical review without waiting for school failure.
recognize: Differences may include joint attention, reciprocity, gestures/language pragmatics, repetitive movements/interests, insistence on sameness and sensory responses.
Some children mask or present later, especially when language/cognition are strong or social demands increase.
differentiate: Hearing impairment, language disorder, intellectual disability, ADHD/anxiety and trauma can overlap or coexist.
Lack of eye contact alone neither diagnoses nor excludes autism.
assessment: Ask developmental history, caregiver/school observations, language/social reciprocity, repetitive/sensory behaviours, regression, adaptive function and strengths.
workup: Use validated screening when appropriate and obtain hearing assessment/targeted medical-genetic evaluation according to the presentation.
Formal diagnosis is multidisciplinary/specialist depending local pathways.
management: Refer early for developmental assessment and supports; services should target communication, participation, regulation and family goals rather than normalization for its own sake.
medicationSafety: Medication does not treat core autism traits; use it only for clearly defined coexisting symptoms with appropriate monitoring.
counselling: Use neurodiversity-respecting language and emphasize strengths plus support needs.
followUp: Track access to diagnostic and therapy/education supports and reassess coexisting ADHD, anxiety, sleep and feeding issues.
examTrap: Ruling out autism because the child is verbal or makes eye contact—or diagnosing it from one screening score alone.
oneLinePearl: Autism screening opens the diagnostic/support pathway; it does not close the diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society autism and developmental resources

title: Pediatric ADHD: Developmental History, Multiple Settings, and Functional Targets
bottomLine: ADHD is a persistent developmentally inappropriate pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity causing impairment in more than one setting. Rating scales support assessment but do not replace developmental history, collateral information and evaluation for sleep, learning, anxiety, mood, trauma and other mimics.
recognize: School/home impairment, task completion, impulsivity, organization and emotional regulation concerns are common.
Symptoms must be interpreted against developmental expectations and not only classroom convenience.
differentiate: Sleep disorders, learning/language problems, anxiety/depression, trauma, autism and substance use can mimic or coexist.
Mania is episodic change with decreased sleep need/other mood features, not a chronic childhood attention pattern.
assessment: Obtain history from child/caregiver and school when possible, developmental/learning history, sleep, mood/anxiety, trauma, substances, cardiovascular/family history and functional goals.
workup: No routine lab/neuroimaging test diagnoses ADHD; test specific mimics or learning needs as indicated.
management: Use behavioural/environmental and school supports plus stimulant or non-stimulant medication when indicated, with goals tied to function rather than score normalization.
medicationSafety: Monitor BP/HR, appetite/weight/growth, sleep, mood and misuse/diversion risk; review cardiac red flags before stimulants.
Do not escalate dose around an untreated learning/sleep problem without reassessing the diagnosis.
counselling: Discuss secure storage, school accommodations and realistic functional targets without framing ADHD as laziness.
followUp: Review benefit and adverse effects with collateral functional data and adjust the multimodal plan.
examTrap: Diagnosing ADHD from one parent rating scale when symptoms occur only at home during severe sleep deprivation.
oneLinePearl: ADHD requires persistent cross-setting impairment, not one high questionnaire score.
sourceBasis: CADDRA Canadian ADHD Practice Guidelines
Canadian Paediatric Society ADHD resources

title: Childhood Asthma: Confirm Variable Airflow Disease and Prevent Future Risk
bottomLine: Childhood asthma is variable respiratory symptoms plus evidence of variable airflow limitation when age permits objective testing. Treatment targets current control and future exacerbation risk, with inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy, device technique and a written action plan central to safety rather than repeated rescue bronchodilator use alone.
recognize: Recurrent wheeze/cough/dyspnea varying over time and triggers supports asthma, especially with atopy/family history.
Viral-triggered preschool wheeze has a broader differential and objective spirometry may not be feasible.
differentiate: Foreign body, airway anomaly, CF, bronchiectasis, aspiration, cardiac disease and dysfunctional breathing can mimic difficult asthma.
Poor control may reflect technique/adherence/exposure rather than insufficient medication.
assessment: Assess symptom frequency/night waking/activity, exacerbations/systemic steroids/ED visits, triggers, smoke/vape exposure, atopy, inhaler/spacer technique and adherence.
workup: Use spirometry with bronchodilator testing when developmentally feasible; use age-appropriate diagnostic pathways for preschool children rather than forcing adult spirometry criteria.
management: Use current Canadian pediatric asthma stepwise treatment with an ICS-containing controller strategy appropriate to age/severity and step up only after checking diagnosis, technique, adherence and exposures.
Provide an action plan and treat acute exacerbations based on severity/response.
medicationSafety: Monitor growth and local ICS effects without undertreating dangerous asthma; rinse/spacer technique reduces some effects.
LABA is not used without ICS as asthma controller therapy.
counselling: Teach spacer/device use, trigger reduction and action-plan zones; ensure school/caregivers know rescue access.
followUp: Reassess control, exacerbation risk, technique and growth after therapy changes.
examTrap: Escalating controller dose before watching the child demonstrate inhaler/spacer technique—or treating repeated rescue-only use as adequate asthma care.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric asthma control begins with the right diagnosis, ICS-containing prevention and correct delivery.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society pediatric asthma guidance
Canadian Paediatric Society acute asthma resources

title: Pediatric Respiratory Infections: Age, Work of Breathing, Hydration, and Syndrome
bottomLine: Most pediatric respiratory infections are viral and supportive-care illnesses, but age, work of breathing, oxygenation, hydration and focal bacterial syndromes determine who needs testing, antibiotics or hospital-level care. Treat the child’s physiology, not the label 'cold'.
recognize: Tachypnea, retractions, grunting, apnea, poor feeding/dehydration and hypoxemia determine severity across syndromes.
Infants can deteriorate with less impressive cough or fever than older children.
differentiate: Bronchiolitis is a clinical infant syndrome where routine antibiotics, bronchodilators and chest radiographs are generally low-value in typical disease.
Croup, asthma, pneumonia, pertussis, foreign body and bacterial tracheitis require different management clues.
assessment: Assess age, respiratory rate/work, SpO2, hydration/feeding, fever duration, focal chest findings, stridor/wheeze, apnea, immunization and high-risk comorbidity.
workup: Avoid routine chest x-ray/viral panels in uncomplicated typical disease when results will not change care; test/image when severity, focal findings or diagnosis require it.
management: Use supportive care for viral URIs/bronchiolitis and syndrome-specific therapy for croup, asthma or bacterial pneumonia when criteria are met.
Escalate hypoxemia, apnea, dehydration or exhaustion.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary antibiotics and OTC cough/cold medicines in young children; dosing must be weight/age appropriate.
counselling: Teach hydration, nasal care when useful, fever comfort measures and concrete breathing/feeding return precautions.
followUp: Reassess persistent/worsening symptoms or new focal findings rather than extending empiric antibiotics for presumed viral illness.
examTrap: Ordering a chest x-ray and antibiotics for every infant with typical bronchiolitis despite stable oxygenation and hydration.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric respiratory infection, severity is work of breathing plus oxygenation plus hydration.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society bronchiolitis, croup and respiratory infection resources

title: Pediatric Gastrointestinal Disorders: Hydration, Growth, and Surgical Red Flags
bottomLine: Pediatric GI complaints are interpreted through age, hydration, growth and abdominal red flags. Most acute gastroenteritis needs oral rehydration rather than testing/antibiotics, while bilious vomiting, peritonitis, GI bleeding, severe dehydration or obstruction patterns demand urgent evaluation.
recognize: Vomiting/diarrhea risk is driven by fluid loss relative to body size and ability to drink.
Chronic abdominal pain with growth failure, blood, nocturnal symptoms, persistent vomiting or inflammatory signs is not a functional diagnosis until evaluated.
differentiate: Bilious vomiting in an infant/child raises obstruction/malrotation concern; forceful progressive nonbilious vomiting in a young infant suggests pyloric obstruction pattern.
Constipation, functional abdominal pain and gastroenteritis are common but should not explain systemic red flags.
assessment: Assess intake/output, weight change, hydration/perfusion, pain location/tempo, stool/blood, vomiting colour, fever, travel/exposure, medications and growth trajectory.
workup: Use stool/labs/imaging selectively based on severe disease, blood, duration, travel, immunocompromise or surgical differential; routine testing is unnecessary for uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis.
management: Use oral rehydration for mild-moderate dehydration when safe and continue age-appropriate nutrition.
Escalate shock, severe dehydration, bilious vomiting, peritonitis or surgical disease and treat identified chronic GI pathology.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine antimotility agents in young children and unnecessary antibiotics for uncomplicated watery diarrhea.
Antiemetics are age/indication specific and do not replace hydration assessment.
counselling: Teach oral rehydration strategy, urine/alertness monitoring and signs requiring urgent reassessment.
followUp: Recheck growth and symptoms in chronic/recurrent complaints and close GI referral/testing loops.
examTrap: Treating bilious vomiting as gastroenteritis because diarrhea occurred earlier—or ordering stool cultures for every uncomplicated acute diarrhea case.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric GI reasoning starts with hydration, growth and whether the abdomen could be surgical.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society acute gastroenteritis/oral rehydration resources
Canadian pediatric GI practice principles

title: Pediatric Skin Conditions: Morphology, Distribution, Child Wellness, and Safety
bottomLine: Pediatric skin diagnosis depends on lesion morphology, distribution, age and whether the child is systemically well. Treat common eczema, impetigo and fungal/viral conditions appropriately, but escalate purpura with illness, blistering/mucosal disease, rapidly spreading infection or neonatal vesicles.
recognize: Atopic dermatitis is chronic pruritic inflammatory skin disease requiring barrier care and anti-inflammatory treatment, not antibiotics unless secondary infection is present.
Impetigo, tinea, molluscum, viral exanthems and contact/irritant dermatitis have distinct morphology/distribution patterns.
differentiate: Nonblanching petechiae/purpura in an ill child differs from benign dermatitis.
Eczema herpeticum, SJS/TEN, staphylococcal scalded skin and invasive bacterial infection require urgent pathways.
assessment: Describe primary lesion, distribution, mucosa, itch/pain, fever/systemic symptoms, medication/exposure history, immune status and newborn age.
workup: Most common rashes are clinical diagnoses; culture/scrape/biopsy only when infection, fungal disease, atypical/refractory process or serious disorder warrants it.
management: Use skin-barrier care and topical anti-inflammatory treatment for eczema, cause-specific antimicrobial therapy for confirmed/suspected infection and avoidance of triggers when relevant.
medicationSafety: Use topical corticosteroid potency/site/duration appropriate to age and body area; avoid chronic unnecessary topical antibiotics or combination products.
counselling: Teach moisturization, appropriate medication use and infection warning signs without steroid phobia.
followUp: Reassess refractory/recurrent disease for adherence, diagnosis, infection, allergy/contact factors or specialty referral.
examTrap: Giving antibiotics to every weeping eczema flare—or calling a febrile child’s nonblanching rash 'viral' without assessing sepsis risk.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric dermatology, morphology plus how sick the child is determines urgency.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society dermatology/infectious-disease resources
Canadian dermatology pediatric practice principles

title: Childhood Fever: Age and Appearance Change the Threshold
bottomLine: Fever is a sign, not a diagnosis. Age, appearance, immunization, immune status and source determine risk; a febrile young infant has a lower threshold for invasive-bacterial-infection evaluation, while a well immunized older child with a clear viral syndrome often needs supportive care rather than broad testing.
recognize: Young infants can have invasive bacterial infection despite relatively well appearance.
Toxic appearance, poor perfusion, respiratory distress, petechiae/purpura, meningismus or focal neurologic change outweigh the numeric fever height.
differentiate: Fever without source, fever with a focal syndrome and fever in immunocompromise have different testing thresholds.
Teething does not explain a significant true fever or systemic illness.
assessment: Confirm age, duration, immunization, exposures, urine/respiratory/GI/neuro symptoms, hydration, perfusion, mental status, rash and high-risk medical history.
workup: Use age-specific febrile-infant pathways and source-directed testing; avoid routine CBC, urine, x-ray or antibiotics for every well older child with an obvious viral syndrome.
management: Stabilize sepsis/meningitis physiology immediately, use age-risk algorithms for young infants and provide supportive/targeted care for low-risk older children.
medicationSafety: Antipyretics are for comfort, not prevention of febrile seizures, and dosing must be weight-appropriate.
Do not alternate multiple fever medicines reflexively when it increases dosing error risk.
counselling: Teach hydration, comfort measures and specific return precautions; explain that fever height alone does not determine severity.
followUp: Provide reliable follow-up for children managed without a definitive diagnosis, especially early in illness.
examTrap: Ordering broad sepsis testing for every well school-age child with a viral URI—or reassuring a young infant solely because they look well.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric fever, age and physiology matter more than the number on the thermometer.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society febrile young infant statement updated 2026
Canadian pediatric fever practice resources

title: Acute Otitis Media: Diagnose the Bulging Drum Before Prescribing
bottomLine: Acute otitis media requires acute symptoms plus middle-ear effusion and tympanic-membrane inflammation, especially a bulging membrane or new otorrhea. Mild appropriately diagnosed AOM in selected children can be observed with reliable follow-up; otitis media with effusion alone should not trigger antibiotics.
recognize: Bulging, opaque/yellow or hemorrhagic tympanic membrane and reduced mobility support bacterial AOM far more than erythema alone.
Otorrhea from a perforated TM supports AOM when external otitis is excluded.
differentiate: Otitis media with effusion has fluid without acute middle-ear inflammation and is not treated with antibiotics.
Otitis externa produces canal tenderness/inflammation rather than a bulging middle ear.
assessment: Assess age, pain, fever/systemic illness, duration, recurrent AOM, immune/craniofacial risk, perforation/tubes and ability to assure follow-up.
workup: AOM is a clinical otoscopic diagnosis; routine labs/imaging are unnecessary for uncomplicated disease.
Evaluate mastoid/postauricular complications when swelling, displacement or systemic illness is present.
management: Use analgesia for all; use observation/delayed prescription for selected mild disease with reliable follow-up and antibiotics for severe/systemically ill or otherwise indicated cases using current Canadian guidance.
Recurrent/persistent effusion with hearing/language impact warrants hearing/ENT pathways.
medicationSafety: Avoid broad-spectrum antibiotics when amoxicillin is appropriate and review true allergy history.
Do not use decongestants/antihistamines as routine AOM cure.
redFlags: Infant under 6 months with concerning illness
counselling: Teach pain control and the 24–48 hour reassessment plan when observation is chosen.
followUp: Reassess non-improvement/worsening and track hearing/language concerns with persistent effusion.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because the tympanic membrane is red during a viral URI without confirming effusion/bulging.
oneLinePearl: For AOM, the bulging drum matters more than the red drum.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society — Management of acute otitis media in children six months of age and older, reaffirmed 2024

title: Pediatric Pharyngitis: Test the Child With a GAS Pattern, Not Every Sore Throat
bottomLine: Most pediatric pharyngitis is viral. Test for group A streptococcus when the age and clinical pattern create meaningful pretest probability, confirm microbiologically before antibiotics in usual low-ARF-risk settings, and recognize deep-neck infection or airway compromise early.
recognize: Fever, moderate-severe sore throat, tender anterior cervical nodes, tonsillar inflammation/exudate and absence of cough/rhinorrhea raise GAS probability.
GAS pharyngitis is uncommon under age 3 outside outbreaks/scarlet fever contexts.
differentiate: Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis or oral ulcers favour viral disease; positive culture in a viral syndrome may represent carriage.
Peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess causes muffled voice, trismus, unilateral swelling, neck stiffness or toxic appearance.
assessment: Assess age, fever, cough/rhinorrhea, swallowing, hydration, voice, neck motion/swelling, rash and community ARF risk.
workup: Use RADT/culture according to pretest probability and local high-ARF-risk context; ASO titres do not diagnose acute GAS pharyngitis.
management: Use supportive care for viral disease and guideline-directed penicillin/amoxicillin therapy for confirmed GAS in usual settings.
Escalate airway/deep-neck infection concern urgently.
medicationSafety: Avoid antibiotics for low-probability viral disease and account for local macrolide/clindamycin resistance in true severe penicillin allergy.
counselling: Explain why testing reduces unnecessary antibiotics and provide return precautions for worsening swallowing/neck/respiratory symptoms.
followUp: Reassess clinical failure and distinguish recurrent infection from GAS carriage when episodes repeat.
examTrap: Treating based on Centor score alone without microbiologic confirmation in a usual low-risk setting.
oneLinePearl: Clinical score selects who to test; the test helps decide who has GAS.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society — Group A streptococcal pharyngitis practical guide

title: Childhood Exanthems: Rash Pattern Plus How Sick the Child Is
bottomLine: Childhood exanthems are usually diagnosed from rash morphology/distribution, fever timing, mucosal findings, immunization/exposure history and overall appearance. Nonblanching purpura, toxic appearance, mucosal blistering or high-consequence vaccine-preventable disease changes the pathway immediately.
recognize: Measles, varicella, roseola, parvovirus, scarlet fever and hand-foot-mouth disease have characteristic but overlapping patterns.
Rash after fever resolution and rash during fever can imply different syndromes.
differentiate: Petechiae/purpura with systemic illness can represent invasive infection rather than benign viral exanthem.
Drug eruptions, Kawasaki disease/MIS-C, SJS/TEN and meningococcemia can mimic infectious exanthems and require different urgency.
assessment: Assess vaccination, travel/contact, fever timing, conjunctivitis/cough/coryza, oral lesions, itch/pain, blanching, mucosa, hemodynamics and immune status.
workup: Typical mild exanthems often need no labs; suspected measles/high-consequence infection requires infection-control and public-health testing before routine waiting-room exposure.
management: Provide supportive care for benign viral disease and disease-specific treatment/PEP/public-health action when indicated.
Isolate and escalate serious/toxic presentations promptly.
medicationSafety: Avoid aspirin in viral illnesses unless a specific pediatric indication exists and avoid unnecessary antibiotics for viral rash.
counselling: Teach contagion/return-to-school rules according to the confirmed/suspected disease and local public-health guidance.
followUp: Reassess atypical/prolonged rash or evolving systemic symptoms.
examTrap: Calling all febrile rashes viral without checking blanching, mucosa, vaccination/exposure and toxic appearance.
oneLinePearl: The rash matters; the child’s physiology matters more.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society infectious disease resources
Public Health Agency of Canada vaccine-preventable disease guidance

title: Pediatric Murmurs: Innocent Pattern or Structural Heart Disease?
bottomLine: Most childhood murmurs are innocent, but cyanosis, abnormal pulses, feeding/exercise intolerance, failure to thrive, syncope, pathologic heart sounds or a harsh/loud/diastolic murmur require structural evaluation. Newborn murmurs deserve a lower threshold for careful oxygenation/pulse assessment and referral.
recognize: Innocent murmurs are typically soft, systolic and occur in a well child with normal growth, pulses and oxygenation.
Critical congenital heart disease may present with poor feeding, tachypnea, shock or cyanosis rather than a dramatic murmur.
differentiate: A flow murmur from fever/anemia differs from fixed structural disease but the underlying cause still needs context.
Syncope during exertion with a murmur is not an innocent-murmur scenario.
assessment: Assess prenatal/newborn history, feeding/growth, cyanosis, exercise tolerance, chest pain/syncope, family sudden death, pulses/BP, SpO2, S2/clicks and murmur timing/location/radiation.
workup: Do not reflexively order ECG/CXR for every classic innocent murmur; obtain echocardiography/cardiology assessment when pathologic features or uncertainty warrants it.
management: Reassure confidently when innocent features are established; refer suspected structural disease and urgently assess cyanosis/shock/heart-failure physiology.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe endocarditis prophylaxis solely because any murmur exists; prophylaxis depends on the confirmed lesion/risk.
counselling: Explain why an innocent murmur is a sound, not heart disease, when criteria are reassuring.
followUp: Reassess if symptoms develop or murmur characteristics change; close cardiology results.
examTrap: Ordering prophylactic antibiotics for dental work because a child has an innocent murmur.
oneLinePearl: A pediatric murmur is interpreted with pulses, oxygenation, growth and symptoms—not volume alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian pediatric cardiology practice resources
Canadian Paediatric Society child health resources

title: Pediatric Orthopedic Conditions: Age, Gait, Growth Plate, and Infection Red Flags
bottomLine: Pediatric musculoskeletal complaints require age-specific localization and attention to growth plates. A limping or non-weight-bearing child with fever, severe pain or joint-motion restriction is septic arthritis/osteomyelitis until appropriately excluded; many rotational/developmental variants need reassurance rather than imaging.
recognize: Transient synovitis, Osgood-Schlatter, nursemaid’s elbow and developmental rotational variants are common but diagnosis depends on age/pattern.
SCFE, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis and malignancy are high-consequence mimics of routine pain.
differentiate: Hip pathology can refer pain to the knee; always examine the hip in unexplained pediatric knee/thigh pain.
SCFE is more likely in adolescents with hip/groin/knee pain and externally rotated gait and requires urgent non-weight-bearing orthopedic care.
assessment: Assess trauma, fever, night pain, weight-bearing, gait, joint ROM, swelling, neurovascular status, growth/development and systemic symptoms.
workup: Image the suspected area when trauma, SCFE, infection, persistent focal pain or other structural concern warrants it; avoid routine imaging for classic benign rotational variants.
management: Urgently escalate suspected septic joint, SCFE, compartment syndrome or neurovascular injury.
Use age-specific conservative care/rehab for benign overuse/developmental conditions and refer persistent deformity/function loss.
medicationSafety: Analgesia is appropriate and should not be withheld to preserve examination; weight-based dosing and NSAID contraindications apply.
redFlags: Fever plus refusal to bear weight
counselling: Explain expected developmental variants and why certain limps need urgent evaluation despite minor or absent trauma.
followUp: Reassess unresolved limp/pain and ensure fracture/infection/orthopedic follow-up.
examTrap: Diagnosing knee strain without examining the hip in an adolescent with limp and referred knee pain from SCFE.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric orthopedics, age and gait localize the problem—and fever plus no weight bearing is urgent.
sourceBasis: Canadian pediatric orthopedic and emergency practice principles

title: Adolescent Health and Confidentiality: Private Time, Capacity, Safety, and Trust
bottomLine: Adolescent care should routinely include private, developmentally appropriate time and a clear explanation of confidentiality and its limits. Decision-making follows capacity and applicable law rather than age alone; safety threats, abuse or mandatory-reporting triggers can limit confidentiality.
recognize: Confidential care improves disclosure around sexual health, substances, mental health, identity and violence.
Parents/caregivers remain important supports but should not automatically hear every competent adolescent disclosure.
differentiate: Confidentiality is not secrecy without limits; serious imminent harm, child-protection obligations and other legal requirements can require disclosure.
Capacity is decision-specific and assessed clinically/legal-contextually rather than presumed solely from chronological age.
assessment: Provide private time, explain limits before sensitive questions and assess home/school, peers, sexuality, substance use, mood/suicide, violence, safety, strengths and goals.
workup: Testing follows the clinical issue—pregnancy/STI/substance or other concerns—and privacy of billing/portals/results should be considered.
management: Engage the adolescent in decisions, involve caregivers with permission when helpful, and act on safety/mandatory-reporting concerns transparently whenever possible.
medicationSafety: Discuss medication privacy, adherence, contraception/pregnancy and overdose risk when relevant.
counselling: Tell adolescents what will remain private and exactly what circumstances require involving others.
followUp: Use confidential contact methods when safe and ensure referrals preserve privacy appropriately.
examTrap: Promising absolute confidentiality before asking about suicide or abuse—or automatically excluding parents from every decision regardless of capacity/preferences.
oneLinePearl: Trust grows when confidentiality limits are explained before they are needed.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society adolescent health/confidentiality resources
Provincial/territorial consent and privacy law

title: Pediatric Mental Health Screening: Screen, Assess Safety, and Confirm the Syndrome
bottomLine: Mental-health screening identifies concern but does not establish a diagnosis. Any positive or concerning presentation requires assessment of symptoms, function, developmental context, family/school factors, substances, trauma and suicide/self-harm safety before choosing treatment or referral.
recognize: Depression/anxiety may present as irritability, school decline, somatic symptoms, sleep problems or withdrawal rather than adult-style verbalized sadness/worry.
Suicide risk can occur without a high screening score and must be assessed directly when clinically indicated.
differentiate: ADHD, learning issues, sleep disorders, autism, trauma, substance use and medical conditions can mimic or coexist with mood/anxiety symptoms.
Normal developmental distress differs from persistent impairment or safety risk.
assessment: Use validated age-appropriate screeners plus interview, caregiver/youth collateral, function, school, sleep, trauma, substances, eating symptoms and direct suicide/self-harm questions.
workup: Medical testing is targeted to plausible contributors, not a routine psychiatric lab panel.
management: Use psychotherapy/family/school supports and medication when diagnosis/severity support it; urgent psychiatric/ED care for unsafe, psychotic, manic or severely impaired youth.
medicationSafety: Monitor activation, suicidality, mania and age-specific adverse effects after psychotropic changes; secure potentially lethal medications when acute risk is present.
counselling: Normalize help-seeking and explain that a screening result is a starting point, not a permanent label.
followUp: Set concrete early follow-up after treatment changes and track function/safety, not score alone.
examTrap: Starting an SSRI from a positive depression screen without asking about suicide risk or past mania.
oneLinePearl: Screening finds risk; clinical assessment finds the diagnosis and safety plan.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society mental-health resources
Canadian child and adolescent psychiatric practice principles

title: Child Maltreatment: Recognize, Stabilize, Document Objectively, and Report When Required
bottomLine: When child maltreatment is suspected, first address urgent medical safety, preserve a neutral trauma-informed history/examination, document objectively and follow provincial or territorial child-protection reporting law. The clinician does not need proof before making a required report, and should not conduct repeated forensic interviewing beyond the medical need.
recognize: Injuries inconsistent with development/history, patterned bruising/burns, sentinel injuries in infants, unexplained fractures, neglect, sexual-abuse concerns or exposure to severe caregiver IPV can raise concern.
A normal genital examination does not exclude child sexual abuse.
differentiate: Accidental injuries and medical mimics exist; consult child-maltreatment expertise when pattern interpretation is complex.
Medical assessment and forensic investigation have different purposes; avoid leading or repetitive questioning.
assessment: Stabilize injuries, obtain a minimal open-ended medical history, assess immediate safety/siblings, perform full examination and document exact statements/findings objectively.
workup: Use age/injury-specific imaging, labs, STI testing or specialized sexual-abuse evidence collection according to current child-maltreatment pathways and timing.
management: Report reasonable suspicion as required by local child-protection law and coordinate pediatric child-maltreatment, social-work and law-enforcement/forensic services as appropriate.
Provide trauma-informed medical care and safety planning regardless of whether abuse is ultimately substantiated.
medicationSafety: Treat pain and medical conditions appropriately; do not sedate or medicate a child simply to facilitate non-urgent forensic questioning.
counselling: Explain the clinician’s safety/reporting responsibilities honestly and avoid blaming the child or non-offending caregiver.
followUp: Ensure medical, mental-health and child-protection follow-up is coordinated and results are communicated to the responsible team.
examTrap: Waiting for certainty or a confession before making a legally required child-protection report.
oneLinePearl: Child maltreatment reporting is based on reasonable concern, not courtroom proof.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society Child and Youth Maltreatment resources
CPS sexual-abuse statement reaffirmed January 2026
Provincial/territorial child-protection legislation

title: Pediatric Toxicology: Exposure, Dose, Time, Physiology, and Poison-Centre Guidance
bottomLine: Pediatric poisoning assessment starts with ABCs, substance/product, formulation, maximum possible dose, child weight, time and symptoms. Contact the regional poison centre early for clinically important or uncertain exposures; do not induce vomiting or apply a generic decontamination rule to every ingestion.
recognize: Small children can have severe toxicity from seemingly few tablets depending on drug; adolescents may have intentional multi-substance overdose requiring suicide assessment.
Button batteries, high-powered magnets, caustics, hydrocarbons, opioids and selected cardiovascular/diabetes drugs have specific high-risk pathways.
differentiate: A witnessed benign taste differs from unknown-dose access to a highly toxic product.
Delayed toxicity is possible with modified-release preparations, acetaminophen and some other agents despite initial wellness.
assessment: Stabilize ABCs/glucose, identify exact product/concentration, estimate maximum dose per kg, timing, co-ingestants, symptoms and intent/access circumstances.
workup: Use agent-specific ECG, glucose/electrolytes, acetaminophen concentration or other testing per poison-centre/toxicology guidance; avoid indiscriminate tox screens that do not change management.
management: Call poison centre for significant/uncertain exposure and follow substance-specific observation, antidote/decontamination and disposition guidance.
Intentional poisoning requires mental-health/safety evaluation before discharge.
medicationSafety: Activated charcoal, antidotes and gastric decontamination have specific indications/contraindications; do not use routinely.
Dose all emergency medications by current pediatric weight/agent protocol.
counselling: Teach locked medication/chemical storage and poison-centre access without shaming caregivers.
followUp: Ensure delayed-toxicity testing/observation and psychosocial follow-up are completed.
examTrap: Inducing vomiting after an ingestion or sending home a well child after a potentially delayed toxic dose without poison-centre guidance.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric toxicology, the product, dose per kilogram and clock determine the plan.
sourceBasis: Canadian poison-centre pediatric toxicology practice
Health Canada poisoning prevention resources

title: Pediatric Allergy: Identify the Trigger, Separate Intolerance, Prepare for Anaphylaxis
bottomLine: Pediatric allergy diagnosis depends on a reproducible exposure-reaction history; positive sensitization tests without compatible symptoms do not equal clinical allergy. Anaphylaxis is treated immediately with IM epinephrine and emergency observation, while chronic food/allergic disease needs avoidance, nutrition and specialist planning without unnecessarily broad restriction.
recognize: IgE-mediated reactions usually occur rapidly with hives/angioedema, respiratory, GI or cardiovascular symptoms after exposure.
Food intolerance and non-IgE syndromes have different timing/mechanisms and should not automatically receive an anaphylaxis label.
differentiate: Viral urticaria is common; isolated chronic hives usually are not caused by one food.
Sensitization on skin/blood testing does not prove clinical allergy without history or supervised challenge context.
assessment: Document exact food/drug/exposure, dose, timing, reproducibility, symptoms, cofactors, asthma control and prior epinephrine use; assess nutrition/growth when foods are avoided.
workup: Use targeted specific-IgE/skin testing and oral challenge under specialist conditions when indicated; avoid broad food panels in nonspecific symptoms.
management: Treat anaphylaxis with IM epinephrine first and activate emergency care; prescribe autoinjector/action plan and allergist referral for confirmed/high-risk allergy.
Manage rhinitis/eczema/asthma as distinct allergic comorbidities.
medicationSafety: Antihistamines do not replace epinephrine for anaphylaxis.
Weight-appropriate autoinjector selection and school/caregiver training matter.
redFlags: Poorly controlled asthma with food allergy
counselling: Teach label reading, epinephrine technique and safe nutrition without expanding avoidance beyond confirmed risks.
followUp: Reassess changing food allergy over childhood and maintain current emergency plans/school forms.
examTrap: Using diphenhydramine as first-line treatment for anaphylaxis—or diagnosing ten food allergies from a broad positive panel without compatible reactions.
oneLinePearl: Clinical reaction defines allergy; epinephrine defines first-line anaphylaxis treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society allergy/anaphylaxis resources
Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology practice guidance

title: Pediatric Endocrine Disorders: Growth, Puberty, Glucose, and Adrenal-Thyroid Emergencies
bottomLine: Pediatric endocrine disease often presents as an abnormal trajectory—growth, puberty, weight or glucose—rather than a single symptom. Interpret labs using age/puberty context and recognize DKA, adrenal crisis, severe hypo/hyperthyroid disease and salt/water disorders as urgent physiology.
recognize: Type 1 diabetes may present with polyuria/polydipsia, weight loss or DKA; growth failure can precede other hypothyroid/celiac/endocrine symptoms.
Precocious/delayed puberty requires age/sex-development context rather than adult hormone ranges.
differentiate: Obesity with preserved/increased linear growth differs from endocrine obesity with slowed height velocity.
Normal pubertal variation differs from progressive virilization, neurologic symptoms or very early puberty.
assessment: Plot growth, assess pubertal stage, symptoms of diabetes/thyroid/adrenal disease, medications, family timing and neurologic signs.
workup: Use age/puberty-specific glucose, thyroid, adrenal, gonadal or growth testing according to phenotype; avoid broad endocrine panels for isolated nonspecific fatigue.
management: Treat DKA/adrenal crisis through emergency pediatric protocols and refer persistent growth/puberty/endocrine abnormalities to pediatric endocrinology.
Support chronic diabetes/thyroid care with family/school planning.
medicationSafety: Insulin and steroid dosing are pediatric/condition specific; never stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes during illness without an expert sick-day plan.
Chronic glucocorticoids can suppress growth/HPA function and require taper/stress planning.
redFlags: Rapid neurologic change with endocrine symptoms
counselling: Explain growth/puberty trends in developmentally appropriate language and avoid weight stigma.
followUp: Track growth/puberty and disease-specific labs with pediatric endocrine support.
examTrap: Ordering cortisol/thyroid/growth-hormone panels for every child with obesity despite normal or accelerated height growth.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric endocrine disease is often a trajectory problem before it is a lab problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society endocrine/diabetes resources
Diabetes Canada pediatric diabetes guidance

title: Pediatric Neurologic Conditions: Development, Localization, Seizure Safety, and Regression
bottomLine: Pediatric neurologic assessment integrates development, age-specific examination, localization and tempo. First seizure, focal deficit, severe headache, weakness or regression requires cause-directed evaluation; status epilepticus, meningitis, raised intracranial pressure and acute focal deficits are emergencies.
recognize: Febrile seizure, epilepsy, migraine, developmental disorders and benign movement phenomena are common but age/phenotype dependent.
Regression, persistent focal weakness, ataxia or altered consciousness is not a benign developmental variation.
differentiate: Syncope can include brief jerks and should not automatically be labelled epilepsy.
Simple febrile seizures differ from prolonged/focal/recurrent-within-illness seizures that warrant broader evaluation.
assessment: Assess development/baseline, event witness history, fever/infection, head trauma, medications/toxins, focal deficits, gait, headache pattern and family neurologic history.
workup: Check glucose/metabolic causes when acute; use EEG/imaging/LP according to event type and red flags rather than routinely after every simple febrile seizure.
management: Treat ongoing seizure/status immediately, stabilize suspected CNS infection/stroke/raised ICP and arrange neurologic referral for unprovoked/recurrent/focal disease.
Provide age-specific seizure/headache safety plans.
medicationSafety: Antiseizure agents have age, interaction, pregnancy/adolescent and monitoring considerations; do not abruptly stop chronic therapy without a plan.
counselling: Teach seizure first aid and when emergency care is needed; avoid unnecessary activity restrictions after low-risk events.
followUp: Close EEG/imaging/specialty results and monitor development/school function.
examTrap: Ordering CT and EEG for every simple febrile seizure—or diagnosing epilepsy from one syncopal event with brief jerks.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric neurology is development plus localization plus tempo.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society neurologic/febrile-seizure resources
Canadian pediatric neurology practice principles

title: Pediatric Urgent-Care Triage: Appearance, Breathing, Circulation, Hydration, and Age
bottomLine: Pediatric triage prioritizes physiology over the chief complaint. Rapidly assess appearance/mental status, work of breathing, circulation/perfusion, hydration and age-specific risk, then stabilize first and refine the diagnosis second; infants can become critically ill with subtle early findings.
recognize: Abnormal interaction/tone, severe retractions/grunting/apnea, cyanosis, delayed perfusion, weak pulses, altered consciousness or inability to drink are high-risk signals.
Young age lowers the threshold for escalation in fever, respiratory symptoms, trauma and dehydration.
differentiate: A high fever in an interactive hydrated child is different from modest fever with poor perfusion/lethargy.
Tachycardia may reflect fever, pain or dehydration but persistent tachycardia after correction can signal serious disease.
assessment: Use a pediatric rapid assessment/ABCs, vitals including appropriate BP/SpO2, weight, glucose when altered, hydration, pain, age, comorbidity and caregiver concern.
workup: Testing follows the stabilized syndrome; do not delay airway/breathing/circulation intervention for complete history or imaging.
management: Escalate airway obstruction, respiratory failure, shock, seizure, anaphylaxis, sepsis, severe dehydration or major trauma immediately.
For dischargeable children, ensure caregiver capacity, clear return precautions and reliable follow-up.
medicationSafety: Use weight-based emergency dosing and equipment; verify weight/maximum doses and avoid decimal/tenfold errors.
counselling: Explain why disposition depends on physiology and age, and give concrete return signs rather than 'come back if worse'.
followUp: Ensure pending results, reassessment windows and specialty referrals have named ownership.
examTrap: Prioritizing the diagnostic label over a child who is becoming less responsive with worsening work of breathing.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric triage, stabilize the child you see before naming the disease you suspect.
sourceBasis: Canadian pediatric emergency-care and resuscitation practice principles
Canadian Paediatric Society acute-care resources
